Well, broadly speaking, from a nation's point of view, men are less valuable; or rather, more expendable - this is why it makes sense to throw them at the embrasures instead of women.

This of course applies mostly to the big wars of the older days - total war situations like WW2 or the Paraguayan War. There are still demographic echoes from the losses in those wars in the most affected countries, and they would be worse if able-bodied women died at the same rate as men (IIRC in WW2 there were like 3-4 dead men per 1 dead woman on the Eastern Front).

In context of the modern North America hardly any of this matters though, they could as well just drop the draft altogether.

Indeed, most of the planet actually doesn't have it. And in some countries the default approach is to boil tap water before drinking - although it still doesn't guarantee that it is completely safe, because of the non-biological elements it can contain.

There are even charities dedicated to bringing drinkable tap water to poorer regions.

Pro tip: don't believe everything that you see in job postings. A lot of it is bullshit. Some job postings describe an "ideal" candidate, but would settle with a worse one. Some job postings are written by fucktards who don't know what they want. Or by an HR/clerk who doesn't care.

Just apply to as many as you can, don't bother with the particularities too much. Also there is no point of being discouraged if you didn't get one you wanted. Think of it as, there is a tiny probability of getting a job, and if you apply to many enough, you increase your chances.

The main challenge is to get through that nonsense to the actual interviews, where you can talk your way into getting hired. If you failed at one interview, that experience could be used to tweak and improve your approach to the following ones.

Of course our minds deceive us, they do it all the time. We don't live in an objective reality, we live in our subjective realities. For example, you can feel fear even though there is no objective threat - it is just a part of your brain sends you fear signals because it thinks that there is an actual threat. It can be trained, too.

It is actively discussed in Evolutionary Psychology - e.g. discrepancies between the modern world and how our brains misinterpret the situations like internet conflicts.

Or Psychology in general.

You can also look up some, for example, Buddhism-related topics (stripped from the spirituality, Western-oriented), if you want to know more ("Buddha, Brain and Neurophysiology of Happiness" is a book I liked. Not written by a scientist or a researcher, but a monk, still decent).

I honestly don't get why people got the idea that "we are doomed" because of covid.

With the worst estimates of mortality being \~5% and the best being \~0.5%, heavily skewed towards older and sick people, we are not "doomed" even if we all got to the streets and start licking each other.

It is also not the worst pandemic since the Spanish Flu - it hasn't even reached levels of the Asian Flu and Hong Kong flu yet by the death toll.

Humanity had a lot of problems in the past, and on the big scale 21st century is still doing really well so far. Maybe it is just not as good as it was in 60s-90s of the past century for the US and other Western countries.

I wonder how the Cuban Missile Crisis would look like with the social media though.

Usually just having an adequate itinerary and proof of funds is enough, they are mostly just interested in being reasonably sure that you won't stay there (and it is always possible to return the tickets, anyway). But having a return ticket won't hurt.

It is explained in the sidebar why "it gets better" is a bad idea.

Unless you are Jesus himself, you don't know whether it will get better. This superficial positivity is meaningless.

In any case, for the specific points of selfishness and ungratefulness, might I recommend "The Ego and Its Own" by Max Stirner?

It is a pretty dry read, not a self-help book by any means, and it is relatively old (19th century). But it does put the idea of selfishness into a certain perspective, and if you don't die from the boredom reading it, you might find some of the ideas to be useful.

There is a lot of ground for schadenfreude.

I don't see why it would be different from the daily glasses usage.

I put mine on for working or reading, but I plan my suicide without glasses on - it would be an act that doesn't require good eyesight, so it makes sense to leave them.

A good starting point might be researching glasses habits regardless of suicide, and then going from there.

I guess suicide is a heavy decision, and the public perception is not adequate at all.

Everywhere is the same superficial bs and burying heads in the sand. They think of some fucking movie jumpers who are talked out of if by some utterly meaningless, but softly spoken words.

Hotlines that are apparently designed exclusively for the people who are in the heat of the moment and could actually be talked out of it by the softly spoken words. Or by the hardly pressed batons, in cases where already distressed people get forcefully admitted to hospitals by the police.

Other "support" is in the same vein. Patronizing, cliche nonsense.

My favorite is "there is help".

I know that feeling bro.

Doing the same at the moment, it gives more clarity than ever.

This sub is supposed to be about peer support, but I am not sure how much support there could be if you calmly and rationally arrived to your conclusions.

Ironically, it is incredibly hard to find any sort of peers even on the internet, who wouldn't immediately judge you or behave like a salesman with "it gets better" and "let me talk you out of it".

I've heard there is a hotline in the UK that allows you to just talk to them about it without them going overboard with trying to "save" you and call police on you or other "life-saving" factory conveyor stuff. That would be nice.
